items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of autonomous AI agents in enterprise environments has introduced a novel software supply chain challenge: dynamic tool integration via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Unlike traditional API integrations with static trust boundaries, MCP enables agents to discover, negotiate, and invoke external tools at runtime, creating an attack surface that existing software security methodologies do not adequately address. This paper presents the first systematic threat taxonomy and defensive methodology for MCP-based tool integration in agentic AI systems. We identify four categories of supply chain threats specific to MCP tool ecosystems: (1) prompt injection via tool descriptions and schema metadata, (2) capability escalation through chained tool invocations, (3) data exfiltration through unmonitored tool output channels, and (4) poisoned tool registries that serve compromised MCP server endpoints. For each threat category, we formalize the attack model and characterize the conditions under which exploitation succeeds. We propose three complementary defensive patterns: Capability Provenance Verification (CPV), which cryptographically attests the origin and integrity of tool capabilities across the MCP lifecycle; Tool-Call Sandboxing with Output Sanitization (TSOS), which enforces isolation and content filtering at the agent-tool boundary; and Registry Attestation Protocol (RAP), which establishes chain-of-trust verification for MCP server discovery. We implement these patterns in a reference MCP Authorization Enforcement Gateway and evaluate against a catalog of 120 simulated attack scenarios spanning all four threat categories. Results demonstrate an 87.5% overall threat detection rate with sub-0.15 ms median enforcement latency and 0% false positive rate across 500 benign operations, while an ablation study confirms that all three patterns are necessary for comprehensive coverage. We discuss implications for enterprise MCP adoption and propose extensions to the MCP specification to support native security metadata.</jats:p>
title: Secure Tool Integration Patterns for Agentic AI Systems: A Software Supply Chain Approach to Model Context Protocol Governance

items.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The possibility of performing complex data analysis through sets of cooperating personal smart devices has recently encouraged the definition of new distributed computing paradigms. The general idea behind these approaches is to move early analysis towards the<jats:italic>edge</jats:italic>of the network, while relying on other intermediate (<jats:italic>fog</jats:italic>) or remote (<jats:italic>cloud</jats:italic>) devices for computations of increasing complexity. Unfortunately, because both of their distributed nature and high degree of modularity, edge-fog-cloud computing systems are particularly prone to cyber security attacks that can be performed against every element of the infrastructure. In order to address this issue, in this paper we present SMCP, a Secure Mobile Crowdsensing Protocol for fog-based applications that exploit lightweight encryption techniques that are particularly suited for low-power mobile edge devices. In order to assess the performance of the proposed security mechanisms, we consider as case study a distributed human activity recognition scenario in which machine learning algorithms are performed by users’ personal smart devices at the edge and fog layers. The functionalities provided by SMCP have been directly compared with two state-of-the-art security protocols. Results show that our approach allows to achieve a higher degree of security while maintaining a low computational cost.</jats:p>
title: SMCP: a Secure Mobile Crowdsensing Protocol for fog-based applications

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of agentic AI systems in enterprise environments has introduced unprecedented complexity and novel security risks, particularly as protocols like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) become foundational for tool integration and agent collaboration. Traditional threat modeling frameworks, such as STRIDE and PASTA, fall short in capturing the layered, dynamic, and cross-protocol vulnerabilities unique to these systems. To address this gap, this thesis presents a comprehensive, workflow-centric risk assessment framework that extends the MAESTRO threat modeling methodology with quantitative metrics. By systematically mapping detected vulnerabilities in MCP and A2Aenabled workflows to the seven layers of MAESTRO, the framework introduces two novel metrics: the Workflow Exploitability Index (WEI) and the Risk Propagation Score (RPS). These metrics quantify both the ease of exploitation and the potential for cascading risk across complex agentic workflows. The framework is validated using adapted real-world and synthetic workflows, demonstrating its ability to prioritize high-risk scenarios that traditional tools overlook. This work establishes a foundation for protocol-aware, quantitative security assessment in agentic AI, enabling organizations to proactively identify, prioritize, and mitigate emerging threats.</jats:p>
title: Towards secure agentic workflows: a MAESTRO-based assessment framework for Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent Protocol

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models and Agentic Artificial Intelligence stand poised to completely overhaul our collective approach to science. Within chemical property prediction in particular, natural language-based workflows for modeling are already making serious inroads. To further this aim, in this white paper we introduce Chemprop-MCP, a Model Context Protocol that makes calling the Chemprop property prediction software possible using LLMs. The application of Chemprop-MCP is demonstrated on a recently curated aqueous solubility benchmark, showing promise for its future applications. Chemprop-MCP is permissively licensed and available via GitHub at https://github.com/chemprop/chemprop-contrib/tree/main/chemprop_contrib/mcp.</jats:p>
title: The Chemprop Model Context Protocol

items.abstract: <jats:p>This research presents a new framework for clinical summarization that combines the TinyLlama model with MIMIC-III and FHIR data using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Unlike cloud-based models like Med-PaLM, our approach uses local processing to cut costs and protect patient data with AES-256 encryption and strict access controls, meeting HIPAA and GDPR standards. It retrieves FHIR-compliant data from public servers (e.g., \texttt{hapi.fhir.org}) for interoperability across hospital systems. Tested on discharge summaries, it achieves ROUGE-L F1 scores of 0.96 for MIMIC-III and 0.84 for FHIR, beating baselines like BioBERT (0.61, p < 0.001) due to efficient preprocessing and MCP’s accurate data grounding. ROUGE, BLEU and BERTScore metrics, along with visualizations, confirm its reliability. The entire pipeline code is available at \url{https://github.com/shekhar-ai99/clinical-mcp} for transparency and reproducibility.</jats:p>
title: A Framework for Secure and Interoperable Clinical Summarization Using the Model Context Protocol: Integrating MIMIC-III and FHIR with TinyLlama
